claim: Liver fibrosis and subsequent cirrhosis are two leading causes of liver disease-related deaths worldwide.
source: Liver fibrosis and subsequent cirrhosis, two leading causes of liver disease-related deaths worldwide (Karlsen et al., 2022), develop as a result of chronic liver injury of multiple etiologies (Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karlsen et al., 2022 and Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021

claim: Liver fibrosis develops as a result of chronic liver injury of multiple etiologies.
source: Liver fibrosis and subsequent cirrhosis, two leading causes of liver disease-related deaths worldwide (Karlsen et al., 2022), develop as a result of chronic liver injury of multiple etiologies (Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021

claim: Fibrosis is characterized by excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins forming fibrous scar tissue.
source: Fibrosis is characterized by excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins forming fibrous scar tissue.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about fibrosis pathology

claim: Pathological matrix in the liver is deposited by activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and/or portal fibroblasts (PFs) in response to inflammatory reaction.
source: In the liver, such pathological matrix is deposited by activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) and/or portal fibroblasts (PFs) in response to the inflammatory reaction (Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021; Henderson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021 and Henderson et al., 2020

claim: Multi-omics studies have framed fibrosis as a dynamic multicellular process associated with remodeling of gene expression landscapes.
source: Recent multi-omics studies have framed fibrosis as a dynamic multicellular process associated with the remodeling of gene expression landscapes (Ramachandran et al., 2019) and profound changes in liver protein abundance as well as composition (Niu et al., 2022; Massey et al., 2017; Klaas et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramachandran et al., 2019

claim: Fibrosis is associated with profound changes in liver protein abundance and composition.
source: Recent multi-omics studies have framed fibrosis as a dynamic multicellular process associated with the remodeling of gene expression landscapes (Ramachandran et al., 2019) and profound changes in liver protein abundance as well as composition (Niu et al., 2022; Massey et al., 2017; Klaas et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Niu et al., 2022; Massey et al., 2017; Klaas et al., 2016

claim: Hepatocellular injury alters parenchymal mechanical properties.
source: Hepatocellular injury alters parenchymal mechanical properties (Georges et al., 2007), thus further facilitating activation of resident HSCs and PFs and their differentiation into myofibroblasts depositing collagen-rich ECM (Olsen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Georges et al., 2007

claim: Altered parenchymal mechanical properties facilitate activation of resident HSCs and PFs and their differentiation into myofibroblasts depositing collagen-rich ECM.
source: Hepatocellular injury alters parenchymal mechanical properties (Georges et al., 2007), thus further facilitating activation of resident HSCs and PFs and their differentiation into myofibroblasts depositing collagen-rich ECM (Olsen et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2011

claim: Accumulation of abnormal ECM promotes ECM-depositing myofibroblasts and fosters progressive whole-organ stiffening as a result of ongoing fibrogenesis.
source: Accumulation of abnormal ECM further promotes ECM-depositing myofibroblasts and fosters progressive whole-organ stiffening as a result of ongoing fibrogenesis (Saneyasu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saneyasu et al., 2016

claim: ECM-associated changes are increasingly perceived as causative, rather than consequential, in fibrosis pathogenesis.
source: Thus, ECM-associated changes are increasingly perceived as causative, rather than consequential, and multiple efforts have focused on the identification of extracellular niche components that drive the pathogenesis of fibrosis (Schiller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schiller et al., 2015

claim: The ECM is a complex network of hundreds of proteins acting as a three-dimensional scaffold, supporting cells mechanically and functioning as a reservoir for secreted factors.
source: The ECM is a complex network of hundreds of proteins acting as a three-dimensional scaffold, supporting cells mechanically and functioning as a reservoir for secreted factors (e.g. growth factors and cytokines) (Hynes, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hynes, 2009

claim: The matrisome consists of 'core matrisome' (structural components of the ECM) and 'matrix-associated matrisome' (ECM-interacting proteins).
source: This so-called 'matrisome' consists of 'core matrisome' (the structural components of the ECM, i.e. collagens, glycoproteins, and proteoglycans) and 'matrix-associated matrisome' (the ECM-interacting proteins) (Naba et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Naba et al., 2012

claim: Transitions of extracellular factors between the insoluble matrisome and the soluble pools modulate their signaling capabilities and bioavailability.
source: Transitions of extracellular factors between the insoluble matrisome and the soluble pools modulate their signaling capabilities and bioavailability (Schiller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schiller et al., 2015

claim: Chronic liver injury is inflicted either by hepatotoxic or by cholestatic insult.
source: In terms of etiology, chronic liver injury is inflicted either by hepatotoxic or by cholestatic insult (Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kisseleva and Brenner, 2021

claim: Iterative carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) intoxication causes hepatocellular damage, HSC activation, and development of pericentral liver fibrosis that evolves into severe bridging fibrosis.
source: Thus, frequently used iterative carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) intoxication causes hepatocellular damage, HSC activation, and development of pericentral liver fibrosis that evolves into severe bridging fibrosis (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2013

claim: 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC) feeding induces obstructive cholestasis, characterized by expansion of PFs and consecutive periportal fibrosis with typical portal-portal septa.
source: In contrast, 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC) feeding induces obstructive cholestasis, characterized by expansion of PFs and consecutive periportal fibrosis with typical portal-portal septa (Fickert et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fickert et al., 2007

claim: Liver fibrosis can be ameliorated by either targeting progression or promoting resolution.
source: As both human and animal studies have shown that liver fibrosis can be ameliorated by either targeting progression or promoting resolution (Trautwein et al., 2015), experimental models have become instrumental for identifying factors and mechanisms central to blocking fibrosis progression and promoting the reversal of advanced fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Trautwein et al., 2015

claim: The study quantified 4734 proteins approximately evenly distributed across all time points and fractions.
source: Using the two models, we quantified 4734 proteins approximately evenly distributed across all time points and fractions (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: 184 matrisome constituents were identified among the quantified proteins.
source: We identified 184 matrisome constituents (Naba et al., 2012; Shao et al., 2020) among the quantified proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Naba et al., 2012 and Shao et al., 2020

claim: Principal component analysis revealed clear temporal separation of CCl4- and DDC-derived samples in both Total and E-fraction.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed clear temporal separation of CCl4- and DDC-derived samples in both Total and E-fraction (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: Samples separated in time, demonstrating fibrosis development and its partial resolution for Total and E-fraction samples in both models.
source: Samples also separated in time, which demonstrated fibrosis development and its partial resolution for Total and E-fraction samples in both models (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: 762 proteins were found to be shared by the CCl4 and DDC models during fibrogenesis.
source: In total, 762 proteins were found to be shared by the two models, while 514 (CCl4) and 1074 (DDC) proteins were identified as unique for the respective model (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 514 proteins were identified as unique for the CCl4 model during fibrogenesis.
source: In total, 762 proteins were found to be shared by the two models, while 514 (CCl4) and 1074 (DDC) proteins were identified as unique for the respective model (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 1074 proteins were identified as unique for the DDC model during fibrogenesis.
source: In total, 762 proteins were found to be shared by the two models, while 514 (CCl4) and 1074 (DDC) proteins were identified as unique for the respective model (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The pro-proliferative mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway showed signaling attenuation in the course of CCl4 treatment but upregulation in the case of DDC treatment.
source: Interestingly, the pro-proliferative mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway showed signaling attenuation in the course of CCl4 treatment but upregulation in the case of DDC treatment, suggesting hyperplastic potential of the DDC model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The DDC model has hyperplastic potential.
source: Interestingly, the pro-proliferative mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway showed signaling attenuation in the course of CCl4 treatment but upregulation in the case of DDC treatment, suggesting hyperplastic potential of the DDC model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from mTOR pathway upregulation data

claim: Analysis of the DDC signature revealed inhibition of tumor suppressor gene Rb1 with simultaneous activation of potential oncogenic regulators KDM5A, MRTFA, MYC, and YAP.
source: Consistently, analysis of the DDC signature revealed inhibition of tumor suppressor gene Rb1 with simultaneous activation of potential oncogenic regulators lysine demethylase 5A (KDM5A), myocardin-related transcription factor A (MRTFA), myelocytomatosis oncogene (MYC), and yes-associated protein (YAP), thus underscoring a potential carcinogenic risk of cholestatic model (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The DDC cholestatic model has a potential carcinogenic risk.
source: Consistently, analysis of the DDC signature revealed inhibition of tumor suppressor gene Rb1 with simultaneous activation of potential oncogenic regulators lysine demethylase 5A (KDM5A), myocardin-related transcription factor A (MRTFA), myelocytomatosis oncogene (MYC), and yes-associated protein (YAP), thus underscoring a potential carcinogenic risk of cholestatic model (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inferred from oncogenic regulator activation data

claim: The CCl4 signature indicated activation of epidermal growth factor (EGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) with simultaneous downregulation of HNF4A.
source: By contrast, the CCl4 signature indicated activation of epidermal growth factor (EGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) with simultaneous downregulation of the HNF4A (Figure 2B), thus supporting previous reports on the importance of these factors during hepatotoxic injury (Kömüves et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous studies

claim: Ineffective downregulation of profibrotic signaling in the DDC-induced model suggested a limited capacity of the liver to heal from cholestatic injury.
source: While dynamic changes of regulatory networks and signaling pathways correlated well with fibrosis progression in both models, ineffective downregulation of profibrotic signaling in the DDC-induced model suggested a limited capacity of the liver to heal from cholestatic injury (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from signaling pathway analysis data

claim: 303 proteins shared by CCl4 and DDC Total proteomes were annotated with matrisome-related keywords and as 'cell adhesion', 'fibrinogen complex', 'platelet aggregation', and 'intermediate filaments'.
source: This revealed that 303 proteins shared by CCl4 and DDC Total proteomes were annotated not only with matrisome-related keywords but also as 'cell adhesion', 'fibrinogen complex', 'platelet aggregation', and 'intermediate filaments', thus indicating engagement in cellular interaction with ECM (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and annotation analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: 452 proteins uniquely identified in CCl4 matrisome-enriched clusters were associated with inflammatory response.
source: As anticipated, 452 proteins uniquely identified in CCl4 matrisome-enriched clusters were also associated with inflammatory response, a well-described feature of this model (Ghallab et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Ghallab et al., 2019

claim: A group of 496 proteins exclusive for DDC was found to associate with 'basement membrane' (BM) and 'cell substrate junction'.
source: A group of 496 proteins exclusive for DDC was found to associate with 'basement membrane' (BM) and 'cell substrate junction' reflecting an increased abundance of BM components synthesized during the development of periductal fibrosis (e.g. laminins, α-chains of collagen types IV, VI, and XVIII; Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Collagen type VI was upregulated during fibrogenesis in both CCl4 and DDC models.
source: In contrast to previous reports (Klaas et al., 2016), we found collagen type VI, a protein regulating ECM contractility (Williams et al., 2020), upregulated during fibrogenesis in both models (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citations

claim: Collagen type I accumulated at the sites of primary injury and was only partially reduced upon recovery in the DDC model.
source: Collagen type I accumulated at the sites of primary injury and, consistent with proteomics, was only partially reduced upon recovery in the DDC model (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Fibronectin abundance in Total CCl4 and DDC proteomes decreased with healing, but IF analysis revealed persisting deposits within capillarized hepatic sinusoids even after a recovery period of 10 days.
source: Although fibronectin abundance in Total CCl4 and DDC proteomes decreased with healing, IF analysis revealed persisting deposits within capillarized hepatic sinusoids even after a recovery period of 10 days (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by proteomics and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C

claim: BM-associated collagen type IV accumulated around fibrotic septa in both models and its persistent presence indicated incomplete liver healing after DDC withdrawal.
source: Consistent with a report on human cirrhotic livers (Mak et al., 2013), BM-associated collagen type IV accumulated around fibrotic septa in both models and its persistent presence indicated incomplete liver healing after DDC withdrawal (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and citation to Mak et al., 2013

claim: Lysyl hydroxylase (Plod3) was found among newly expressed CCl4-specific proteins.
source: Notably, we found lysyl hydroxylase (Plod3), a matrisome protein highly expressed in activated HSCs (Nishio et al., 2019), among newly expressed CCl4-specific proteins.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Nishio et al., 2019

claim: DDC-specific matrisomal proteins included elastin (ELN), a proposed PF marker.
source: In contrast, DDC-specific matrisomal proteins included elastin (ELN), a proposed PF marker (Yang et al., 2021; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Yang et al., 2021

claim: A set of 18 proteins quantified from the signature of hepatocytes exhibited faster decline in the hepatotoxic CCl4 than DDC model.
source: A set of 18 proteins quantified from the signature of hepatocytes exhibited faster decline in the hepatotoxic CCl4 than DDC model (Figure 4A), corresponding well to the extensive parenchymal injury evidenced by high alanine and aspartate transaminase levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Rapid increase in HSC and activated PF signatures paralleled the activation and proliferation of ECM-depositing myofibroblasts in both fibrotic models.
source: Rapid increase in HSC and activated PF signatures paralleled the activation and proliferation of ECM-depositing myofibroblasts in both fibrotic models (Figure 4B) evidenced by IF staining of myofibroblast marker alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Faster upregulation of activated PFs in DDC confirms their predominant role in cholestatic fibrosis.
source: However, faster upregulation of activated PFs in DDC confirms their predominant role in cholestatic fibrosis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on PF signatures

claim: Temporal abundance profiles of Kupffer cell, macrophage, monocyte, and B-cell signature proteins illustrate faster recovery from inflammation with healing in the CCl4 than in DDC model.
source: Temporal abundance profiles of Kupffer cell, macrophage, monocyte, and B-cell signature proteins illustrate faster recovery from inflammation with healing in the CCl4 than in DDC model (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Integrin β1 expression increased during fibrosis and likely corresponds to the expansion of HSCs, simultaneously with induced integrin β1 expression on liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and injured hepatocytes.
source: Our profiling revealed increased expression of integrin β1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), the most abundant collagen receptor, which has been reported (together with integrins α1 and α5) to correlate with the stages of human liver fibrosis (Nejjari et al., 2001). Given its cell-type-specific expression prevalence, this finding likely corresponds to the expansion of HSCs, simultaneously with induced integrin β1 expression on liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and injured hepatocytes (Nejjari et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Nejjari et al., 2001

claim: Fibronectin receptor integrin α5 was detected in Total DDC proteome only.
source: Unexpectedly, fibronectin receptor integrin α5 (typically expressed on HSCs, PFs, and LSECs [Olsen et al., 2012; Couvelard et al., 1993]) was detected in Total DDC proteome only (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and citations

claim: Boosted expression of integrin α5 has been reported in liver tumors.
source: Since a boosted expression of integrin α5 has been reported in liver tumors (Lai et al., 2011), this finding further supports the tumorigenic potential of biliary fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2011

claim: Strong induction of TGFβ-activating integrin αv in both CCl4 and DDC Total proteomes reflected its central role in fibrogenesis.
source: Strong induction of TGFβ-activating integrin αv in both CCl4 and DDC Total proteomes (Figure 4E) reflected its central role in fibrogenesis (Reed et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and citation to Reed et al., 2015

claim: In E-fraction, integrin αv was found to increase only in the CCl4 model, suggesting its close association with ECM specifically during hepatotoxic injury.
source: Strikingly, in E-fraction, integrin αv was found to increase only in the CCl4 model (Figure 4E), suggesting its close association with ECM specifically during hepatotoxic injury.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: During CCl4-induced injury, αv staining was enhanced at the periphery of pericentral hepatocytes adjacent to the collagen-rich scars.
source: During CCl4-induced injury, αv staining was enhanced at the periphery of pericentral hepatocytes adjacent to the collagen-rich scars, reflecting ongoing liver periportalization with the injury (Ghallab et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and citation to Ghallab et al., 2019

claim: In DDC-driven cholestasis, antibodies to αv stained strongly with reactive biliary epithelial cells (BECs), the main drivers of fibrogenesis in biliary fibrosis.
source: In DDC-driven cholestasis, antibodies to αv stained strongly with reactive biliary epithelial cells (BECs), the main drivers of fibrogenesis in biliary fibrosis (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F

claim: 1273 (CCl4) and 762 (DDC) differentially expressed proteins were found with at least threefold higher expression in E- than in S-fraction.
source: We found 1273 (CCl4) and 762 (DDC) differentially expressed proteins, defined by at least threefold higher expression in E- than in S-fraction (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Proteins grouped into three (CCl4, 406 proteins) and two (DDC, 63 proteins) ECM-enriched clusters exhibited increasing insolubility during fibrogenesis.
source: Proteins grouped into three (CCl4, 406 proteins) and two (DDC, 63 proteins) ECM-enriched clusters exhibited increasing insolubility during fibrogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: 93 (CCl4) and 16 (DDC) proteins not present in control samples but induced by treatment were identified.
source: Interestingly, we identified 93 (CCl4) and 16 (DDC) proteins not present in control samples but induced by treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Abundance of most of the identified proteins in E-fraction decreased with healing in the CCl4 but not in the DDC model.
source: Abundance of most of the identified proteins in E-fraction decreased with healing in the CCl4 but not in the DDC model (Figure 5B), suggesting model-specific incorporation of matrisome-associated proteins into insoluble ECM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Extracellular matrix protein-1 (ECM1) was among proteins upregulated with disease onset in E-fractions of both fibrotic models.
source: Among proteins upregulated with disease onset in E-fractions of both fibrotic models was extracellular matrix protein-1 (ECM1; Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Weak ECM1 staining in control livers was confined mostly to Kupffer cells and the apical membrane of BECs.
source: Subsequent IF analysis confirmed weak ECM1 staining (corresponding to low expression levels) in control livers, which was confined mostly to Kupffer cells and the apical membrane of BECs (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Increased ECM1 abundance during fibrogenesis was paralleled by its increasing localization within the infiltrating inflammatory cells and activated Kupffer cells.
source: Increased ECM1 abundance during fibrogenesis was paralleled by its increasing localization within the infiltrating inflammatory cells and activated Kupffer cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data

claim: ECM1 heavily decorated apical membranes of BECs forming reactive ductuli in DDC-treated livers.
source: In addition, ECM1 heavily decorated apical membranes of BECs forming reactive ductuli in DDC-treated livers, thus corresponding to higher MS intensity of ECM1 during the development of biliary fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data

claim: Leukocyte-specific integrin β2-interacting protein coronin 1a (CORO1A) displayed a significant positive correlation with fibrogenesis reflecting the time course of the immune response.
source: For example, leukocyte-specific integrin β2-interacting protein coronin 1a (CORO1A) displayed a significant positive correlation with fibrogenesis reflecting the time course of the immune response (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Methionine cycle enzyme adenosylhomocysteinase (AHCY) displayed negative correlation with fibrogenesis corresponding to hepatocellular death induced by fibrogenesis.
source: In contrast, negatively correlating methionine cycle enzyme adenosylhomocysteinase (AHCY) corresponded to hepatocellular death induced by fibrogenesis (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Clusterin was among proteins positively correlating with fibrotic scar development and resolution in both Total and insoluble proteomes.
source: Among proteins positively correlating with fibrotic scar development and resolution in both Total and insoluble proteomes was clusterin (CLU), a glycoprotein implicated in several diseases (Figure 6D; Wilson and Zoubeidi, 2017).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 6D and citation to Wilson and Zoubeidi, 2017

claim: In untreated livers, clusterin was detected in BECs and partially in hepatocytes.
source: In untreated livers, clusterin was detected in BECs and partially in hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data

claim: Upon CCl4 intoxication, IF staining revealed prominent clusterin expression by damaged hepatocytes.
source: Upon CCl4 intoxication, IF staining revealed its prominent expression by damaged hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data

claim: Clusterin increasingly re-localized along the collagen deposits over the healing period in CCl4 model.
source: Strikingly, clusterin increasingly re-localized along the collagen deposits over the healing period.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data

claim: In DDC-treated livers, clusterin was found mostly in BECs forming reactive ductuli and in hepatocytes, with minimal changes upon healing.
source: In DDC-treated livers, clusterin was found mostly in BECs forming reactive ductuli and in hepatocytes, with minimal changes upon healing (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Extracellular clusterin deposition in close proximity of collagen fibers was demonstrated in fibrotic and cirrhotic human livers of various etiologies at different stages of fibrosis.
source: Moreover, extracellular clusterin deposition in close proximity of collagen fibers was further demonstrated in fibrotic and cirrhotic human livers of various etiologies at different stages of fibrosis (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: The gradual increase in clusterin expression with the progression of fibrosis against the background of chronic hepatitis C (METAVIR score F1-F4) emphasized its role in the development of liver fibrotic diseases.
source: The gradual increase in clusterin expression with the progression of fibrosis against the background of chronic hepatitis C (METAVIR score F1-F4) further emphasized its role in the development of liver fibrotic diseases.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from human samples

claim: Identification of 'Rho-A', 'Rho family GTPases', 'actin cytoskeleton', and 'integrin/ILK signaling' among top canonical pathways suggested that the hepatotoxic injury leads to increased cytoskeletal tension in injured hepatocytes.
source: Identification of 'Rho-A', 'Rho family GTPases', 'actin cytoskeleton', and 'integrin/ILK signaling' among top canonical pathways elicited by proteins of Total CCl4 proteome together with the proteins of matrisome-enriched clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C) suggested that the hepatotoxic injury leads to increased cytoskeletal tension in injured hepatocytes.
evidence: Inferred from pathway analysis data

claim: The clusterin promoter comprises binding motifs for mechanosensitive transcription factors such as c-Fos and AP-1/Jun.
source: Interestingly, the clusterin promoter comprises binding motifs for mechanosensitive transcription factors such as c-Fos and AP-1/Jun (Jin and Howe, 1999; Miyamoto-Sato et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin and Howe, 1999 and Miyamoto-Sato et al., 2010

claim: Local clusterin induction can reflect the dynamic changes of microenvironmental mechanical cues.
source: This suggests that local clusterin induction can reflect the dynamic changes of microenvironmental mechanical cues.
evidence: Inferred from mechanosensitive transcription factor binding data

claim: Clusterin overexpression associates with increased activity of ECM-degrading matrix metalloproteinases.
source: As clusterin overexpression associates with increased activity of ECM-degrading matrix metalloproteinases (Shim et al., 2011), we hypothesize that clusterin accumulation facilitates the remodeling and resolution of scar tissue.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shim et al., 2011

claim: Clusterin accumulation facilitates the remodeling and resolution of scar tissue.
source: As clusterin overexpression associates with increased activity of ECM-degrading matrix metalloproteinases (Shim et al., 2011), we hypothesize that clusterin accumulation facilitates the remodeling and resolution of scar tissue.
evidence: Hypothesized based on clusterin's association with matrix metalloproteinases

claim: AFM analysis revealed no substantial topological variations across defined compartments in control livers, with median Young's moduli ranging between 1.2 and 1.6 kPa.
source: Our AFM analysis revealed no substantial topological variations across defined compartments in control livers, with median Young's moduli ranging between 1.2 and 1.6 kPa (Figure 7C, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by AFM measurement data shown in Figure 7C and Table 1

claim: Fibrogenic response triggered progressive tissue stiffening apparent in all analyzed compartments.
source: Fibrogenic response triggered progressive tissue stiffening apparent in all analyzed compartments (Figure 7D–F, Table 1), with collagen-rich regions the stiffest at maximal fibrosis (~4.4 kPa at T2; Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by AFM measurement data shown in Figure 7D-F and Table 1

claim: Collagen-rich regions were the stiffest at maximal fibrosis (~4.4 kPa at T2).
source: Fibrogenic response triggered progressive tissue stiffening apparent in all analyzed compartments (Figure 7D–F, Table 1), with collagen-rich regions the stiffest at maximal fibrosis (~4.4 kPa at T2; Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by AFM measurement data shown in Figure 7D and Table 1

claim: Interface regions exhibited initial softening (T1; median ~0.8 kPa vs. 1.2 kPa in control livers), which was followed by increase in stiffness up to ~2.0 kPa (T2).
source: Unexpectedly, interface regions exhibited initial softening (T1; median ~0.8 kPa vs. 1.2 kPa in control livers), which was followed by increase in stiffness up to ~2.0 kPa (T2).
evidence: Supported by AFM measurement data

claim: With healing (T4), all compartments demonstrated clear decrease in stiffness.
source: With healing (T4), all compartments demonstrated clear decrease in stiffness (Figure 7D–F), although this was only marginal in the regions corresponding to injured hepatocytes.
evidence: Supported by AFM measurement data shown in Figure 7D-F

claim: Significant softening of collagen-rich scar tissue during healing indicated partial resolution of scar-associated ECM.
source: Significant softening of collagen-rich scar tissue during healing indicated partial resolution of scar-associated ECM while it associated with the incorporation of several core matrisome proteins (e.g. COL1A1 and FBN1) into the scar tissue (Figures 1F and 6D).
evidence: Inferred from AFM and proteomic data shown in Figures 1F and 6D

claim: The initial softening of interface hepatocytes upon injury counterbalances the stiffening of the injured hepatocytes and/or fibrous scar tissue regions.
source: An unexpected decrease in the stiffness of interface hepatocytes with the initial fibrotic changes revealed by our AFM analysis suggests that the initial softening of interface hepatocytes upon injury counterbalances the stiffening of the injured hepatocytes and/or fibrous scar tissue regions.
evidence: Inferred from AFM measurement data

claim: Interface hepatocytes undergo a phenotypic shift in response to injury.
source: As the interface hepatocytes have been shown to undergo a phenotypic shift in response to the injury (Ben-Moshe et al., 2022), it will now be interesting to determine whether altered mechanical properties serve as the cue leading to the genetic fetal reprogramming or if this initial softening is due to the expression of fetal markers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ben-Moshe et al., 2022

claim: The nature of liver injury determines the set of components assembled in diseased ECM.
source: We and others have demonstrated that the nature of liver injury determines the set of components assembled in diseased ECM (Klaas et al., 2016), which thus reflects unique features of the injury.
evidence: Supported by citation to Klaas et al., 2016

claim: The initial decline in abundance of hepatocyte- and activated BEC-expressed collagen type XVIII α-1 chain in the hepatotoxic CCl4 model corresponds to hepatocyte death followed by expansion of both collagen type XVIII α-1 chain-expressing cell types.
source: For instance, the initial decline in abundance of hepatocyte- and activated BEC-expressed collagen type XVIII α-1 chain (Schuppan et al., 1998) and its consecutive increase thereafter in the hepatotoxic CCl4 model corresponds to hepatocyte death followed by expansion of both collagen type XVIII α-1 chain-expressing cell types (Manco et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from proteomic data and supported by citations to Schuppan et al., 1998 and Manco et al., 2019

claim: Extensive collagen type XVIII α-1 chain expression in DDC-induced cholestasis was already apparent in the early fibrotic deposits due to a massive ductular reaction.
source: By contrast, extensive collagen type XVIII α-1 chain expression in DDC-induced cholestasis was already apparent in the early fibrotic deposits due to a massive ductular reaction.
evidence: Inferred from proteomic data

claim: Some BM-associated proteins (e.g. collagen type XVIII α-1 chain, collagen type IV and VI α-2 chains, and perlecan) are among the 14-gene signature potently predicting human patient cirrhosis progression and survival.
